questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with a black eschar and surrounding non-pitting oedema. He gives history of handling dead cattle. Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: The classic painless ulcer with black eschar (malignant pustule) and non-pitting oedema following contact with animal hides/carcasses is pathognomonic of cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated hypopigmented scaly plaques on her chest. KOH mount shows short hyphae and clusters of yeast cells ('spaghetti and meatballs'). What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: The description is classic for Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia furfur). Ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 10 days is effective. Terbinafine has poor activity against Malassezia as it is a yeast.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that rupture to form honey-coloured crusts. Similar lesions affect school contacts. Which statement is TRUE regarding this condition?
opts: It can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
It is caused exclusively by Staphylococcus and never leads to renal complications
Topical fusidic acid is ineffective; systemic antibiotics are always required
Bullous form is caused by Streptococcus and non-bullous by Staphylococcus
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) and can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Bullous impetigo is caused by S. aureus phage group II producing exfoliative toxin.

questions.q: A 42-year-old immunocompromised patient has painful vesicles in a dermatomal distribution along left T5. The most serious complication to watch for is:
questions.exp: In immunocompromised patients, the most serious complication of herpes zoster is disseminated zoster (>20 lesions outside the primary dermatome), which can involve visceral organs including lungs, liver, and brain.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man has a painless indurated ulcer on the glans with rubbery consistency and non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is reactive. Which statement is TRUE?
opts: Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate can demonstrate Treponema pallidum
VDRL becomes reactive before the primary chancre appears
Treponema pallidum is routinely cultured on blood agar
questions.exp: Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate from the primary chancre is the gold standard for direct demonstration of Treponema pallidum. VDRL typically becomes reactive 1-4 weeks after chancre appearance. T. pallidum cannot be cultured in vitro.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy with a groove sign (Greenblatt sign). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: The groove sign — a groove between enlarged inguinal and femoral lymph nodes separated by Poupart's ligament — is pathognomonic of Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3.

questions.q: A 35-year-old leprosy patient on MDT develops acute painful erythematous nodules on extensor surfaces with fever and malaise. Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate. Best management is:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL/Type 2 lepra reaction) presents with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic symptoms. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL (100-400 mg/day), especially in males. MDT should NEVER be stopped.

questions.q: A 45-year-old leprosy patient on treatment develops sudden facial palsy, claw hand, and loss of sensation with thickened tender nerve trunks. This represents:
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction most common in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL). It presents with acute neuritis causing nerve function impairment. Prednisolone is the treatment; MDT must be continued.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has butterfly malar erythema, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and joint pain. ANA is strongly positive (1:640). Which antibody is MOST specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the MOST specific antibody for SLE (~25-30% of patients). Anti-dsDNA is more sensitive but less specific. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman has Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, skin tightening of fingers and face, and telangiectasias. The MOST specific serological marker for her condition is:
questions.exp: Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) is most specifically associated with anti-centromere antibody (ACA). Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with dermatomyositis/polymyositis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man has flaccid blisters on normal skin that rupture easily, leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky's sign is positive. DIF shows IgG in an intercellular 'chicken wire' pattern. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets Desmoglein 3 in mucosal-dominant disease and Desmoglein 1+3 in mucocutaneous disease. The intraepidermal blister is suprabasal. Nikolsky's sign is positive. DIF shows IgG in intercellular spaces.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman has tense blisters on an urticarial base on inner thighs and axillae. Nikolsky's sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the DEJ. The correct diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense blisters on urticarial base in elderly patients. Nikolsky's sign is negative (subepidermal blister). DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the DEJ. Target antigens are BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1).

questions.q: A 25-year-old has intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces of elbows, knees, and buttocks. IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase is positive. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at papillary tips. Treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. DIF shows granular IgA at papillary tips. Treatment is dapsone (immediate relief) plus strict gluten-free diet (long-term remission).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly translucent papule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on the alar rim, with central ulceration, after lifelong sun exposure. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (rodent ulcer) presents as a pearly translucent papule with rolled/everted edges, telangiectasias, and central ulceration on sun-exposed areas, most commonly the nose. It is locally invasive and rarely metastasizes.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer has a rapidly growing, indurated, ulcerated nodule on the lower lip with chronic sun exposure and pipe-smoking history. Cervical nodes are enlarged. Which prognostic factor MOST increases metastasis risk in this tumour?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma with perineural invasion (PNI) has the highest risk of metastasis and poor prognosis — PNI is associated with recurrence, nodal metastasis, and reduced survival, and is a high-risk feature per NCCN guidelines.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has multiple hyperpigmented macules, café-au-lait spots, and axillary freckling with a positive family history. The associated tumour causing hypertension with elevated VMA in urine is:
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is associated with phaeochromocytoma, which secretes catecholamines causing episodic hypertension, sweating, and headache. Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the urinary metabolite used for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes patch testing. She develops erythema, papules, and vesicles to nickel sulfate at 48 hours. This reaction represents:
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (delayed-type/cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by CD4+ T cells (Th1). Patch testing reads at 48 and 96 hours. Nickel is the most common contact allergen.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery for BCC, horizontal frozen sections of all peripheral and deep margins are examined intraoperatively. The MAIN advantage over standard wide local excision is:
opts: Higher cure rate with maximum tissue conservation
questions.exp: Mohs surgery achieves the highest cure rate (up to 99% for primary BCC) because it allows complete histological examination of all margins in real-time, enabling maximum conservation of normal tissue while ensuring complete tumour removal.

questions.q: A patient with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis is being started on methotrexate. Which investigation is MOST important to assess before initiating therapy?
opts: LFTs, CBC, renal function, and chest X-ray
questions.exp: Before starting methotrexate, baseline investigations include LFTs, CBC (methotrexate causes bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity), renal function tests (reduced renal function increases toxicity), and chest X-ray (to rule out TB/interstitial lung disease).

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on isotretinoin for severe acne asks about pregnancy precautions. Which statement regarding isotretinoin teratogenicity is MOST accurate?
opts: Teratogenicity risk ends 1 week after stopping
Effective contraception is required from 1 month before, during, and 1 month after treatment
Isotretinoin is safe in the second trimester only
Male partners of female patients need not take precautions
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Effective contraception must be used 1 month before, throughout treatment, and for 1 month after stopping. Common foetal defects include craniofacial, cardiac, and CNS abnormalities.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has vitiligo affecting 40% BSA including the face. Which treatment has the BEST evidence for repigmentation in extensive vitiligo?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB, 311 nm) is the gold standard for extensive/widespread vitiligo, with the best evidence for repigmentation. Topical treatments are more suitable for localised disease. Monobenzone is used for near-total vitiligo to achieve uniform skin colour.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man has well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histology shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, and Munro microabscesses. The basic molecular defect is:
opts: Decreased keratinocyte proliferation with normal maturation
Increased keratinocyte proliferation with impaired differentiation
Melanocyte destruction by cytotoxic T cells
questions.exp: Psoriasis is characterised by markedly increased keratinocyte proliferation (turnover reduced from 28 days to 3-4 days) with impaired terminal differentiation, driven by Th1/Th17 axis and cytokines including IL-17, TNF-α, and IL-23.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman has erythematous indurated plaques with central clearing on malar regions. She is photosensitive. ANA is 1:80; anti-Ro/SSA is positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) presents with photosensitive annular or psoriasiform plaques with central clearing on sun-exposed areas. Anti-Ro/SSA is positive in ~70-80% of SCLE. Unlike DLE it heals without scarring.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man has annular erythematous plaques with fine scales on the trunk following a large herald patch. The most likely diagnosis and causative agent are:
questions.exp: Pityriasis rosea classically begins with a herald patch followed by smaller daughter lesions in a Christmas tree distribution. HHV-7 (and HHV-6) are the most strongly implicated causative agents. It is self-limiting, resolving in 6-8 weeks.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man on hydroxyurea for polycythaemia vera develops painful bilateral medial malleolar ulcers, longitudinal melanonychia, and macrocytosis. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Increase hydroxyurea dose and add topical antibiotics
Discontinue hydroxyurea and switch to an alternative cytoreductive agent
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea-induced leg ulcers at the medial malleolus are a recognised complication in ~8-10% on long-term therapy. Discontinuation of hydroxyurea leads to healing in most cases. Alternative cytoreductive agents (ruxolitinib, anagrelide, interferon) should be considered.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man has recurrent grouped vesicles on the vermilion border, recurring at the same site every few weeks, triggered by stress. The best prophylactic approach to reduce recurrence frequency is:
opts: Topical acyclovir cream applied at first sign
Oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily continuously
questions.exp: Recurrent herpes labialis with frequent episodes (>6/year) is best managed with suppressive oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily continuously. Valacyclovir 500 mg/day is an alternative with better bioavailability.

questions.q: A 19-year-old has comedones, papules, and pustules on the face, back, and chest. Which is the MOST important pathogenic factor in acne vulgaris?
opts: Sebum overproduction leading to follicular plugging and Cutibacterium acnes proliferation
Staphylococcus aureus infection of hair follicles
Type IV hypersensitivity to sebum antigens
questions.exp: The pathogenesis of acne involves four key factors: excess sebum production (seborrhoea), follicular hyperkeratinisation causing comedones, colonisation by Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Sebum production driven by androgens is the initiating factor.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on long-term chloroquine for rheumatoid arthritis is referred for baseline ophthalmological examination. Which ocular side effect is being screened for?
questions.exp: Antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine) can cause irreversible retinal toxicity presenting as bull's eye maculopathy — concentric rings of RPE atrophy around the macula. Hydroxychloroquine is less toxic than chloroquine. Baseline and annual ophthalmological screening is mandatory.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man has multiple soft, painful ulcers with ragged undermined edges and a necrotic base on the prepuce, with tender fluctuant inguinal buboes. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and presents with painful soft ulcers with undermined/ragged edges and tender inguinal buboes (in 50% of cases). Treatment: azithromycin single dose or ciprofloxacin 3 days.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has progressive sclerodactyly, dilated nail-fold capillaries on dermoscopy, Raynaud's phenomenon for 5 years, and dyspnoea on exertion with a restrictive PFT pattern. The most likely pulmonary complication is:
questions.exp: ILD/pulmonary fibrosis is the most common pulmonary complication in diffuse systemic sclerosis, causing a restrictive PFT pattern. HRCT shows ground-glass opacities and honeycombing (NSIP pattern). PAH is more common in limited SSc/CREST and causes reduced DLCO.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman has livedo reticularis, recurrent DVT, and two miscarriages. Anti-cardiolipin IgG antibodies are strongly positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. The most appropriate long-term therapy is:
questions.exp: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) presents with thrombosis and/or obstetric complications with antiphospholipid antibodies confirmed on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart. Long-term anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3 for venous events) is the mainstay of treatment.
